entities.name: Lucius Cassius Longinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Cassius Longinus was consul of the Roman Republic in 107 BC, a pivotal moment in the First Triumvirate, which saw his colleague Gaius Marius, then serving his first of seven consulships. This marked a significant shift in the balance of power within the Roman Republic, as Marius's influence and Longinus's own ambitions began to rival those of the other triumvirate members, Julius Caesar and Pompey. The tensions between these three leaders would eventually lead to the downfall of the Republic and the rise of the Roman Empire. Longinus's involvement in this power struggle highlights the complex web of alliances and rivalries that defined the late Roman Republic.

Longinus was a key figure in the early years of the First Triumvirate, and his actions and decisions had far-reaching consequences for the course of Roman history.

As a consul, Longinus played a role in the governance of Rome, although the exact nature of his involvement is not well documented. It is known that he served alongside Marius, who was instrumental in shaping the Republic's military and political direction.

The legacy of Longinus and the First Triumvirate can be seen in the subsequent rise of the Roman Empire, which would go on to shape the course of Western civilization. The complex interplay of alliances and rivalries between Longinus, Marius, Caesar, and Pompey would have lasting impacts on the development of the Roman state and its institutions.

This moment in history serves as a powerful reminder of the intricate web of relationships that defined the late Roman Republic, and the ways in which individual actions can have far-reaching consequences for the course of human events.
